message.content: Pandas belong to the family Ursidae (bears). Their lineage diverged from other bears around 20–25 million years ago during the Miocene epoch. Fossil evidence suggests that early bear relatives were omnivorous, but the giant panda’s ancestors gradually specialized on bamboo. By the Pliocene (~5–7 Myr ago), the giant panda had evolved its distinctive black‑and‑white coat and a highly modified wrist bone that functions as a pseudo‑thumb, allowing it to grasp bamboo stalks. The modern giant panda (Ailuropoda melanoleuca) first appeared in the fossil record about 2–3 Myr ago. Its diet shifted almost exclusively to bamboo, which led to a reduction in gut size and digestive efficiency compared to other bears. The red panda (Ailurus fulgens), though sharing a name, is not closely related; it belongs to its own family Ailuridae and diverged from the bear lineage earlier, around 30–40 Myr ago. Thus, pandas illustrate a unique evolutionary path within the bear family, marked by dietary specialization and morphological adaptations.
